extracted.intended_audience: general public, media activists, journalists, researchers interested in media consolidation and media democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for analyzing and measuring media concentration and its democratic effects across media sectors (movies, newspapers, magazines, radio, TV, cable, books, Internet). Uses ownership, revenue, audience, regulatory and diversity indicators to evaluate monopoly power and localism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant-corporations (Bagdikian >50% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chart revenue (or other suitable market) numbers for each media category and count the biggest companies whose combined market share exceeds 50 percent of that sector; those companies are counted as the dominant media corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally used by Ben Bagdikian and reapplied by Extra! and others; historical examples show the count falling over time (e.g., 1983: 50 people; 1987: 26; 1993: 20; 2009: 15 for certain sectors). Data sources cited include Advertising Age and Box Office Mojo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of revenue (or circulation) as the metric for dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Base dominance calculations on revenue figures for each media category; when revenue data are not available (historically for newspapers), use circulation as the proxy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagdikian used circulation for newspapers when revenue figures were seldom available; with Advertising Age revenue data (2009) available, revenue can be used across sectors to better reflect market power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include emergent technologies in concentration analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand traditional-sector analyses to include newer distribution/content platforms such as cable television, satellite radio and the Internet when measuring media concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When emergent technologies are added to the analysis the count of dominant corporations can change (the piece notes an expanded analysis including cable, satellite radio and Internet left the dominant count at 20 in one survey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising revenue concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how advertising dollars are distributed across companies and platforms—i.e., which corporations capture the largest shares of advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising is central to the commercial model; example figures: $309 billion spent on ads in 2009. Online ad concentration example: Google and Yahoo received over half of $20.9 billion online ad revenue in 2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical integration and cross-ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which corporations own properties across multiple media industries (infrastructure, content production, distribution) and how that integration concentrates control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Comcast and AT&T seeking both pipes and content; Comcast's purchase of NBC/Universal; many major publishers/companies hold significant assets in multiple media sectors, amplifying market power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion picture industry dominance (box office share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use box-office revenue shares to identify which studios dominate the film industry and whether a handful control the majority of audience/market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In 2009 Warner Brothers, Paramount, Sony/Columbia and 20th Century Fox together accounted for more than 60% of the $10.6 billion box office; the six major studios together took 80% of box office in 2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper concentration (circulation/revenue chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure concentration in newspapers by chain circulation and/or revenue — identify the chains that together distribute or receive over half the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagdikian historically used circulation; 2009 revenue data showed five corporations received over half the industry’s $19.7 billion revenues (Gannett, Tribune Co., NY Times Co., Advance Publications, MediaNews Group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine concentration (advertising revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine concentration in magazine publishing by counting publishers that together control half the magazine advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2009 three companies controlled half of the $12.6 billion of magazine ad revenue; Time Warner held 40% of the market. Large acquisitions (e.g., Hearst buying Hachette titles) further reduce the number of dominant publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio concentration (ownership counts and revenue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate radio consolidation by counting station ownership, following changes in ownership caps, and by measuring revenue share among major radio companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory changes matter: 1996 Telecommunications Act removed most ownership caps. Result: Clear Channel and Sirius XM controlled over half radio revenue in 2009; Clear Channel grew from 43 stations to 850 in U.S. markets since 1995.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network television concentration (broadcast ad revenue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure broadcast television concentration by comparing broadcast TV advertising revenue captured by leading networks/companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For 2009 CBS, News Corp (Fox) and Walt Disney (ABC) took over half of broadcast TV ad revenue; the top four (adding NBC) took 70%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cable television concentration (cable ad revenue and combined TV markets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess concentration in cable networks by their share of cable advertising revenue and consider combined broadcast+cable market concentration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2009 three cable networks (Disney, Time Warner, Viacom) received over half of $49 billion in cable ad revenue. Treated with broadcast TV, four companies would dominate the combined $74 billion market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book publishing concentration (revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which publishing corporations together receive half the revenue from book sales to measure concentration in book publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In 2009 five corporations (Bertelsmann, Pearson, Hachette, News Corp, CBS) controlled half of the $23.9 billion book market; most have holdings in other media industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet concentration (ISP market structure and online ad dominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure both the concentration among Internet service providers (access pipes) and the concentration of online advertising/search market share among major Internet companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most U.S. users may choose only one or two ISPs locally; Comcast was the highest-revenue media company and purchased NBC/Universal. For online ads in 2009, Google and Yahoo received over half of $20.9 billion. Search algorithms shape access and audience flows; academic work (Hindman) suggests online audience concentration can exceed traditional media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and newsroom diversity metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the demographic diversity of media ownership and newsroom staffing (race, gender) as part of assessing whether media serve diverse publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: heads of the 20 dominant corporations are still white males; ASNE statistics: ethnic minorities <13% of newsroom employees, <4% of television station ownership, <8% of radio station ownership; compare to national demographics (2010 census ~36% minority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Localism and audience concentration (availability of local news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how many local news outlets remain in cities and whether audiences have access to multiple local voices; measure whether market conditions produce 'one-paper towns'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major cities like Houston, Seattle, Denver and Cincinnati down to one local daily paper; Internet local content is often disadvantaged relative to national players; localism is a key public-interest indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative democratic standard: diversity of sources and the 'freedom to hear'
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge media systems against the First Amendment-inspired ideal that the widest possible dissemination of information from diverse and antagonistic sources is essential to public welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Justice Hugo Black’s standard as a normative benchmark: assess whether corporate concentration and market practices narrow the range of ideas available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-quality and public-interest obligation assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether consolidation and market incentives lead to lowest-common-denominator programming, neglect of investigative journalism, and failure to meet public-interest responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance notes that vertically integrated companies incline to national, mass-appeal content at the expense of in-depth investigations; internet/blogs currently cannot fully replace well-funded investigative reporting by experienced editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and policy influence on consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Include analysis of how legal and regulatory decisions (FCC rulings, ownership caps, Telecommunications Act provisions, merger approvals) enable or constrain consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 7/7/7 and 15/15/15 ownership rules, the 1996 Telecommunications Act removing most radio caps, the FCC allowing Sirius/XM to merge, and later ownership transactions such as GE selling NBC stake to Comcast.
